newsitem.title: USA: US Congress opens with focus on Gingrich ethics.
newsitem.headline: US Congress opens with focus on Gingrich ethics.

text.p: When the U.S. Congress reconvenes on Tuesday the spotlight will initally focus on embattled House Speaker Newt Gingrich, but meaty issues such as balancing the budget and an overhaul of the Medicare health plan won't be far behind.
"I'm looking forward to resolving (the Gingrich) matter so we can get on the real issues of the day," Senate Democratic Leader Thomas Daschle of South Dakota said on "Face the Nation" Sunday.
Republicans say publicly they expect near-unanimous support for Gingrich's re-election as speaker, but privately they are scrambling to buck up nervous lawmakers.

This partisan brawl over Gingrich, the Georgia Republican who admitted breaking House of Representatives rules and giving false information to an ethics committee, will dominate the first week of Congress and could poison the atmosphere much longer.

The emphasis on ethics was not the opening programme envisioned by majority Republicans, who earlier predicted a two-year session brimming with goodwill and concrete results on budget, tax, health and environmental legislation.
Daschle said he wanted to see the Gingrich matter resolved quickly, so Republicans and Democrats can consider "how we can work together" on issues important to voters.
To do so, Gingrich and Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott hope to shake a negative image of Republicans developed during two government shutdowns last winter.
The leaders want to cooperate with the White House, building on 1996 bipartisan compromises on welfare, health and immigration laws that helped them keep control of Congress.
"We have an absolute moral obligation to make the system work," Gingrich told fellow Republicans in November.

House Republican Whip Tom DeLay said the Gingrich issue would not deter the Republican majority. "We are not going to give up just because the liberal Democrat leadership wants to try to destroy us," he told CNN's "Late Edition with Frank Sesno."
The quest for a balanced budget will dominate the new Congress, as it did during the last session, and Daschle said Sunday important negotiations had already taken place.
"I think there is a real possibilty we can start with a much more bipartisan tone to these negotiations than we saw two years ago when the government was shut down," Daschle said.
President Bill Clinton in February will unveil his budget plan and Republicans have said the time finally may be ripe for a pact to balance the budget by 2002.
Diving into the debate, Congress will vote as early as February on a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution.
The amendment failed by one Senate vote in 1995. Republicans picked up two Senate seats in November, possibly giving them the two-thirds majority they need for passage.
"That's a key indication whether there is going to be a spirit of cooperation or a spirit of collision," said Stephen Moore of the free-market CATO Institute.
"If the balanced budget amendment passes ... that lays the groundwork for a real substantive budget agreement. If the amendment fails then I think all bets are off," he said.

Overhaul of Medicare health care for the aged and a slew of middle-class tax cuts, including reduction of the capital gains rate and an education tax break, will be prime elements of any overall budget deal.
Burned by Democrats accusing them of trying to slash Medicare, Republicans will wait for the White House to take the lead on changes in the insurance programme for the elderly.
"We're in it together or we're not in it at all because Republicans are not going to step out onto every limb we can find like we did in 1995," a House Republican aide said.
Campaign finance reform is another hot item. Republicans will investigate a growing scandal regarding questionable campaign contributions to Democrats from foreign interests.
Democrats will counter with a push for new campaign finance laws. Democrats also want to expand health insurance to children and the unemployed and revamp pension laws.

The House plans another try on a constitutional amendment limiting the terms of members of Congress. The Senate will begin confirmation hearings in January on Clinton Cabinet nominees, including Madeleine Albright as secretary of state.
